background.definition: Primary fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) is a chronic pain syndrome of widespread, bilateral pain along the axial skeleton.

list.listitem: Age-adjusted incidence of FMS: 6.9 cases per 1000 in men and 11.3 cases per 1000 in women.
The prevalence of FMS in the United States is 2%, including 3.4% of women and 0.5% of men.

The rate of work absences for sick days is 61 episodes per 100 person-years for employees with fibromyalgia alone, and approximately 85 to 90 episodes for employees who had cooccurring chronic conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, depression, or other psychiatric disorders.
The pain of FMS cannot be traced to a specific structural or inflammatory cause.
Patients with mood disorders such as depression or anxiety disorders are more likely to have FMS, although no cause-and-effect relationship has been established.
Work stress such as workplace bullying (OR = 4.1), high workload (OR = 2.1), low decision latitude (OR = 2.1) may be a contributing factor in development of FMS.
FMS lacks unique pathophysiological characteristics. Patients with FMS have lower pain thresholds, high pain ratings for noxious stimuli, and altered temporal summation of pain stimuli.
Neuroendocrine axis abnormalities and autonomic nervous system dysfunction have been demonstrated in FMS.

FMS and overlapping conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, headaches, and chronic fatigue syndrome share characteristics that have led researches to suggest the concept of central sensitivity syndrome.

Evaluate for comorbid mood disorders, depression, and/or anxiety. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Joint pain and stiffness in the morning, joint swelling and inflammation, radiological findings, elevated serum markers (eg, ESR, rheumatoid factor [RF])
History of prior infection, inflammation, elevated serum antibodies (eg, Lyme titers)
Major and minor criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome
Proximal muscle weakness, myotonia, precocious cataracts, muscle pain and stiffness

list.listitem: See the ACR 2016 revised fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria ().
Alternatively, see the AAPT diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia ().
Fibromyalgia should be suspected clinically in patients with at least 3 months of widespread pain, moderately severe sleep problems or fatigue, irrespective of other medical diagnoses.
See and for diagnostic criteria.

Currently, there are no specific diagnostic tests that confirm the diagnosis of FMS. To rule out other disorders (eg, inflammatory arthritis, hypothyroidism), consider ordering an ESR, RF, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and CBC.
While patients with fibromyalgia syndrome may have an elevated antinuclear antibody titer, these patients are not predisposed to develop autoimmune disease.
Consider further laboratory tests and imaging when an underlying disease is suspected based on the history and physical examination.
There is limited quality evidence that patients with fibromyalgia have higher levels of IL-6, IL-8, tumor necrosis factor, and c-reactive protein than controls.
The London Fibromyalgia Epidemiology Study Screening Questionnaire () can aid in identifying patients who should have a diagnostic evaluation to rule out FMS.
Suspect fibromyalgia in patients with at least 3 months of widespread pain; rule out structural and inflammatory disorders and apply the ACR criteria to establish the diagnosis ().
Evaluate for comorbid mood disorders, depression, and/or anxiety.

Educate the patient about fibromyalgia syndrome and its management and initiate multimodal therapy: CBT, physical activity (aerobic and strength training), and medication (eg, antidepressants, cyclobenzaprine).
Patients should be educated about the diagnosis of fibromyalgia syndrome. C
Antidepressants effective for FMS, include low-dose TCAs, Aand duloxetine or milnacipran. A
Other effective medications include muscle relaxants, B tramadol, B and pregabalin. A
CBT, Aaerobic or strength-training exercise A benefit patients with fibromyalgia.
Treatment should be multimodal, involving medication, CBT, and exercise. B
A variety of medications have been evaluated and found to be at least somewhat helpful for fibromyalgia. However, medication trials tend to be 3 months or less, so long-term data are limited.

Drug treatments were reviewed by the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) in 2018, using best evidence and a consensus approach. The drugs were assessed by their ability to reduce key fibromyalgia symptoms of pain, fatigue, sleep and improve daily functioning in addition to strength and relevance of evidence (eg, number of trials and patients, effect size, adverse outcomes and cost). Most recommendations were weak for or against use, meaning most clinicians would recommend for or against a treatment, but a substantial minority would not recommend it.
TCAs (eg, amitriptyline 25 mg/d) improve symptoms in patients with FMS (NNT = 4).EULAR reached 100% agreement, concluding “weak (support) for” use of low-dose amitriptyline.
SSRIs (eg, fluoxetine 20 mg/d) improve pain and sleep, although the benefit appears to be less than that of TCAs.EULAR: 94% agreement, weak against.

A meta-analysis of 18 RCTs of antidepressants found them effective in reduction in pain, fatigue, depressed mood, and sleep disturbances with improved health-related quality of life; the effect size was large for TCAs, medium for monoamine oxidase inhibitors, and small for SSRIs.

A Cochrane Review of 18 RCTs involving the SNRIs duloxetine or milnacipran demonstrated that each of these was more effective than placebo in reducing pain, but did not improve fatigue or sleep. EULAR based their conclusions of pain reduction and some benefit on fatigue and disability: 100% agreement, weak for.
Authors of a network meta-analysis found that duloxetine, pregabalin and milnacipran were all more effective than placebo, with duloxetine most likely to provide a benefit.

SNRIs are likely to be the most effective anti-depressant for pain syndromes including fibromyalgia. A Cochrane review/network meta-analysislikewise found duloxetine at standard dose (60mg/d) to be moderately effective for pain, physical function, sleep, quality of life, and patient global impression of change (moderate to high certainty). Milnacipran was the second most effective medication (moderate certainty) across all outcomes.

Another network meta-analysis of 36 studies with over 11,000 patients concluded that amitriptyline was associated with improved sleep (SMD -0.97, 95% CI -1.10 to -0.83), less fatigue (SMD -0.64, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.53), and an improvement in quality of life (SMD -0.80, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.65). Duloxetine at a dose of 120 mg daily resulted in the greatest reduction in pain (SMD -0.33, 95% Cr -0.36 to -0.30) and improvement in depressive symptoms (SMD -0.25, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17) vs placebo.
Mirtazapine does not appear to be more effective than placebo, based on a Cochrane review of 3 studies (n = 606).
Combination therapy with amitriptyline and fluoxetine was more effective than either medication alone.

Cyclobenzaprine (a muscle relaxant) improves symptoms. The minimal effective dosage is 10 mg/d, with titration to 40 mg/d as needed (NNT = 5). EULAR noted high drop-out and adverse-effect rates and only two trials using intention-to-treat analyses: 75% agreement, weak for.
Tramadol/acetaminophen (analgesic combination at 37.5 mg/325 mg) improves pain. The average patient obtaining relief used four tablets per day. EULAR: 100% agreement, weak for.

The anticonvulsant gabapentin may improve pain scores at a dose of at least 1200 mg/d. However, a Cochrane review evaluating gabapentin for the treatment of fibromyalgia only found 1 small RCT and deemed its result to be very uncertain and its evidence to be very low quality.

The anticonvulsant pregabalin improves pain scores at a dose of at least 300 mg/d (NNT = 9). Response is dose dependent, and dosages over 450 mg/d may be required for clinical effectiveness. A Cochrane review found high certainty evidence that pregabalin 300 to 600 mg daily significantly improves pain in 12 to 26 weeks, with tolerable adverse events, among fibromyalgia patients with moderate to severe pain. Furthermore, pregabalin improves other symptoms, quality of life, and function. Overall, its efficacy was deemed similar to duloxetine and milnacipran. Regarding adverse events, majority of fibromyalgia patients, both in active treatment and placebo arms, experienced adverse events (70% to 90%). But particular adverse events were more common in pregabalin, including dizziness (NNTH = 3.7), somnolence (NNTH = 7.4), weight gain (NNTH = 18), and peripheral edema (NNTH = 19). Serious adverse events were similar for pregabalin and placebo. Withdrawals for any reason were higher in pregabalin only for the 600 mg dose in trials of classic design. Finally, withdrawals secondary to adverse events were 10% higher in pregabalin, but withdrawals secondary to lack of efficacy were 6% lower for pregabalin compared to placebo, based on high quality evidence.
A 2025 meta-analysis of RCTs showed that pregabalin or sodium oxybate are likely to improve sleep in patients with fibromyalgia, although data are heterogeneous and trials are of variable quality.
There is no good evidence to support or discourage using clonazepam for fibromyalgia symptoms.
A Cochrane review concluded that based on very low-quality evidence, quetiapine may be helpful for patients with fibromyalgia and major depression.
There are no studies on the use of phenytoin or valproate in fibromyalgia.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence from high-quality trials to establish the efficacy of combination pharmacotherapy versus monotherapy for adults with fibromyalgia.

Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) do not appear to be helpful for fibromyalgia, based on a Cochrane review that only found modest efficacy of NSAIDS based on very low quality evidence from small trials with significant methodological shortcomings.
A Cochrane review found no RCTs evaluating the efficacy of oxycodone as monotherapy or in combination with naloxone for fibromyalgia.

An overview of 21 Cochrane reviews of pharmacologic treatments of fibromyalgia in adults found moderate- to good-quality evidence that duloxetine, milnacipran, and pregabalin were each effective in meaningful pain relief at 4 to 12 weeks. However, longer term effectiveness data are lacking.

Evidence for the effectiveness of acupuncture is mixed. A recent meta-analysis of 6 small RCTs failed to show a significant difference in pain intensity over placebo. Although EULAR agreed that evidence supporting real versus sham acupuncture was less consistent for benefit, they reached 93% agreement, weak for.
EMG-guided biofeedback improves quality of life scores and decreases trigger-point sensitivity.

In a systematic review of chiropractic management of fibromyalgia, the investigators found moderate evidence in support of massage, muscle strength training, acupuncture, and spa therapy (balneotherapy). There was limited evidence to support spinal manipulation, movement/body awareness, vitamins, herbs, or dietary modification.

EULAR recommendations as follows: chiropractic evaluation, 93% agreement, strong against; massage, 86% agreement, weak against; biofeedback, 100% agreement, weak against; spa therapy, 93% agreement, weak for; hypnotherapy, 86% agreement, weak against; meditative movement, 71% agreement, weak for; mindfulness/mind-body therapy, 73% agreement, weak for.
A small RCT demonstrated benefit from woolen underwear and bedding on reducing pain in patients with fibromyalgia.
In one RCT, neither Reiki nor touch was found to improve symptoms or function of patients with fibromyalgia.

A systematic review found that cannabis use is common among patients with fibromyalgia. There is no good quality evidence for the benefit of cannabinoids, based on two low quality studies with a total of 72 participants.
Thermal baths and massage are effective.

In May 2025, the American College of Physicians issued best practice advice on the use of cannabis and cannabinoids for chronic noncancer pain. The guidance recommends advising patients at increased risk of harm—including young or older adults, pregnant individuals, and those with a current or past substance use disorder, including patients with fibromyalgia—to avoid these products. For other patients, clinicians should explain that current evidence suggests only a small potential benefit.

EULAR, based on their identification of 20 reviews with 2494 participants, concluded that strong evidence supports use of aerobic and/or strengthening exercise - either land or water based. This was confirmed by a meta-analysis of 18 studies with 1184 subjects.
Exercise is effective for fibromyalgia.

Supervised aerobic training has beneficial effects on physical capacity and symptoms in fibromyalgia syndrome. Best results appear to be obtained when the exercise program lasts for at least 4 weeks and patients continue exercise after the end of the formal program.

A Cochrane review found aerobic exercise training effective in improving health-related quality of life and all-cause withdrawal (moderate quality evidence), and suggested it may slightly improve pain and physical function, but may not have significant effects for fatigue and stiffness (low quality evidence). However, long-term, aerobic exercise may have minimal or no effects for pain, physical function, and all-cause withdrawal.
Strength training may also have beneficial effects on symptoms. The benefits of flexibility exercise training are unclear.
Mixed exercise (including at least 2 of 3 categories: aerobic, resistance, and flexibility) produces modest improvements in physical function, HRQOL, fatigue, and sleep quality.
Dance-based interventions reduce fibromyalgia impact and pain and improve quality of life, particularly those involving a creative component.

A RCT involving 66 participants with fibromyalgia for a mean of 11 years found that tai chi was more effective than general wellness education in improving pain, function, and symptoms. Another RCT found that compared to aerobic exercise of a similar intensity and duration, tai chi produced similar or greater symptom improvement for up to 52 weeks.
In a meta-analysis of 10 trials, hydrotherapy was found to afford short-term benefit on pain and health-related quality of life in patients with fibromyalgia.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for whole body vibration (WBV) exercise training for fibromyalgia.
Low-level laser therapy may enhance the effects of exercise on fibromyalgia symptoms, but the methodological quality of studies is weak.
Patients should be educated about fibromyalgia syndrome upon diagnosis.
CBT improves patient symptoms when used alone or with pharmacologic treatments. .
Mindfulness interventions are effective.

A Cochrane review of psychological therapies for chronic pain (like fibromyalgia) in adults found small to very small beneficial effects for CBT in improving pain and distress (moderate quality) and disability (low quality).
A Cochrane review also found remotely-delivered CBT to have small beneficial effects for pain (moderate certainty) and disability (moderate to low certainty) among adults with chronic pain .
A 2025 meta-analysis of seven RCTs assessing insomnia targeted CBT showed a significant benefit of CBT on sleep.

A proprietary smartphone app (Stanza) that utilizes acceptance and commitment therapy is superior to monitoring symptoms only to achieve "much improvement" in symptoms (NNT = 5). The app is approved by the Food and Drug Administration.
Educating newly diagnosed patients with FMS can help improve symptoms and patient self-efficacy (exercise, relaxation).

A meta-analysis of 9 trials of multimodal treatment for fibromyalgia demonstrated short-term benefits of reduced pain, fatigue, depressive symptoms and improved quality of life and physical fitness. There was no evidence, however, of long-term efficacy on these measures.

Two RCTs demonstrated that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), when compared to sham rTMS, reduced pain intensity. In one study, rTMS also improved fatigue, sleep, morning tiredness, general activity, and walking, with the benefits lasting up to 25 weeks. Another RCT of 38 patients found that rTMS improved quality of life on the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire compared to sham rTMS after 11 weeks. These effect sizes may be statistically but not clinically significant. A more recent RCT of rTMS found no benefit.

A systematic review identified 14 small studies with 433 participants evaluating rTMS for fibromyalgia and concluded that there was a benefit on pain and quality of life, but not depression or other symptoms.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for fibromyalgia.
Consider referral to a rheumatologist, pain management specialist, physiatrist, or psychiatrist to share management in patients who do not improve.
Fibromyalgia syndrome can be controlled but not cured. C
If untreated, patients with fibromyalgia experience increasing pain and associated depression and anxiety.

feature.caption: American College of Rheumatology 2016 Revised Fibromyalgia Diagnostic Criteria.
feature.feature_body:
Criteria
A patient satisfies modified 2016 fibromyalgia criteria if the following 3 conditions are met:
Widespread pain index (WPI) ≥7 and symptom severity scale (SSS) score ≥5, OR WPI of 4-6 and SSS score ≥9. Generalized pain, defined as pain in at least 4 of 5 regions, must be present. Jaw, chest, and abdominal pain are not included in generalized pain definition. Symptoms have been generally present Symptoms have been generally present for at least 3 months.Symptoms have been Symptoms have been generally present Symptoms have been generally present for at least 3 months.Symptoms have beengenerallypresent A diagnosis of fibromyalgia is valid irrespective of other diagnoses. A diagnosis of fibromyalgia does not exclude the presence of other clinically important illnesses.
Ascertainment
(1) WPI: note the number areas in which the patient has had pain over the last week. In how many areas has the patient had pain? Score will be between 0 and 19.
(Region 1) Left upper region (Region 2) Right upper region (Region 5) Axial region
Jaw, left Jaw, right Neck
Shoulder girdle, left Shoulder girdle, right Upper back
Upper arm, left Upper arm, right Lower back
Lower arm, left Lower arm, right Chest
Abdomen
(Region 3) Left lower region (Region 4) Right lower region
Hip (buttock, trochanter), left Hip (buttock, trochanter), right
Upper leg, left Upper leg, right
Lower leg, left Lower leg, right
(2) Symptom severity scale (SSS) score:
Fatigue
Waking unrefreshed
Cognitive symptoms
For each of the 3 symptoms above, indicate the level of severity over the past week using the following scale:
0 = No problem
1 = Slight or mild problems, generally mild or intermittent
2 = Moderate, considerable problems, often present and/or at a moderate level
3 = Severe: pervasive, continuous, life-disturbing problems
The SSS score: is the sum of the severity scores of the 3 symptoms (fatigue, waking unrefreshed, and cognitive symptoms (0-9) plus the sum (0-3) of the number of the following symptoms the patient has been bothered by that occurred during the previous 6 months:
(1) Headaches (0-1)
(2) Pain or cramps in lower abdomen (0-1)
(3) And depression (0-1)
The final symptom severity score is between 0 and 12.
The fibromyalgia severity (FS) scale is the sum of the WPI and SSS. The FS scale is also known as the polysymptomatic distress (PSD) scale.
From Wolfe F, Clauw DJ, Fitzcharles MA, Goldenberg DL, Häuser W, Katz RL, Mease PJ, Russell AS, Russell IJ, Walitt B. 2016 Revisions to the 2010/2011 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2016 Dec;46(3):319-329.

feature.caption: The London Fibromyalgia Epidemiology Study Screening Questionnaire (LFESSQ).
feature.feature_body:
Pain Criteria (in Last 3 Mo) Response
1. Have you had pain in the muscles, bones, or joints lasing at least 1 wk? Yes No
2. Have you had pain in your shoulders, arms, or hands? On which side? Right, left, or both? R L both No
3. Have you had pain in your legs or feet? On which side? Right, left, or both? R L both No
4. Have you had pain in your neck, chest, or back? Yes No
Fatigue Criteria
1. Over the past 3 mo, have you often felt tired or fatigued? Yes No
2. Does the tiredness or fatigue limit your activities? Yes No
Meeting the Pain Criteria Requires
"Yes" responses to all four pain items, and either: Both a right and a left side positive response. Both sides positive response.
Screening positive for chronic debilitating fatigue requires a "yes" response to both fatigue items.
From White KP, Speechley M, Harth M, Ostbye T. The London Fibromyalgia Epidemiology Study: the prevalence of fibromyalgia syndrome in London, Ontario. J Rheumatol 1999;26:1570-1576.

feature.caption: ACTTION-APS Pain Taxonomy (AAPT) Diagnostic Criteria for Fibromyalgia
feature.feature_body:
Dimension 1: Core Diagnostic Criteria
1. Multisite pain (MSP) defined as 6 or more pain sites from a total of 9 possible sites 1.(had, 2.left arm, 3.right arm, 4.chest, 5.abdomen, 6.upper back and spine, 7.lower back and spine (including buttocks), 8.left leg, 9.right leg)e
2. Moderate to severe sleep problems OR fatigue
3. MSP plus fatigue or sleep problems must have been present for at least 3 months
NOTE: The presence of another pain disorder or related symptoms does not rule out a diagnosis of fibromyalgia. However, a clinical assessment is recommended to evaluate for any condition that could fully account for the patient's symptoms or contribute to the severity of the symptoms.
From Arnold LM, Bennett RM, Crofford LJ, Dean LE, Clauw DJ, Goldenberg DL, Fitzcharles MA, Paiva ES, Staud R, Sarzi-Puttini P, Buskila D, Macfarlane GJ. AAPT Diagnostic Criteria for Fibromyalgia. J Pain. 2019 Jun;20(6):611-628.
